title: Auction Market Theory: How Markets Find Value

lessons.title: The market as a two-way auction
lessons.desc: Watch the first 30 minutes of one ES session on a 1-minute chart. Note two moments where price tried a new level and trading dried up, and one where it kept trading. Label them "rejected" or "accepted".
lessons.descHtml: Watch the first 30 minutes of one ES session on a 1-minute chart. Note two moments where price tried a new level and trading dried up, and one where it kept trading. Label them "rejected" or "accepted".

lessons.desc: Mark the last ten sessions on a 30-minute chart as balance or imbalance days. Next to each, write the range of the balance or the direction of the imbalance. This becomes the starting data for your day-type work in VP-04.

lessons.desc: Pick one balanced session. Draw its high and low after the first hour and count the rotations between them. Record whether the final break of the range was accepted or rejected.

bodyHtml:
Every chart you have studied so far shows the result of an auction. Buyers and sellers keep testing prices to find out where the other side is willing to trade. Auction market theory is a way of reading the chart as that search. It gives you words for what you see: price trying higher, finding no one to sell to, and coming back; or price leaving a range because a new group of traders turned up. Profile and order-flow tools in this track all sit on top of this idea, so it is the right place to start.

This is a framework traders use, not a scientific law. J. Peter Steidlmayer developed it while trading at the Chicago Board of Trade, and the exchange released his Market Profile to the public in 1985. James Dalton and co-authors extended it in Mind Over Markets (listed as further reading below). You don't need to accept every claim made for it to find the vocabulary useful.

The market as a two-way auction

An auction is a process for finding a price at which both sides will trade. In a futures market it runs continuously: buyers post bids, sellers post offers, and trades happen whenever someone accepts a price that is already on offer. How that matching works in detail is the subject of VP-07. For now, one idea is enough.

Price moves in order to find trade. When price rises and buyers keep trading with sellers, the move is being accepted. When price rises and trade dries up, there are no sellers willing to deal at those prices, and no more buyers keen to chase them. The move has gone too far for now. Market Profile practitioners describe this as the market "advertising" a price: it shows a new price, and the amount of trade that follows is the response.

Price advertises, volume confirms

A move to new prices on strong, continuing trade is read as acceptance. A move to new prices that quickly stops trading and returns is read as rejection. You will see both ideas in every later chapter.

Value: where most trade happens

In this framework value is simply the price range where most of the trading took place over a period. It is not a fundamental "fair price" for the S&P 500. It is where buyers and sellers were most willing to do business with each other. Volume and time tell you where that is. The volume profile turns the idea into numbers: the value area is the range holding about 70% of the volume, and the point of control (POC) is the single busiest price. VP-03 shows how to compute both.

Prices far above value are expensive in auction terms: fewer people are willing to trade there, so price tends to move quickly and not stay long. Prices far below value are cheap in the same sense. That is why value edges become reference points. Traders watch whether price is accepted beyond an edge or rejected back into value.

Balance and imbalance

Markets alternate between two states. In balance, buyers and sellers broadly agree on value, and price rotates back and forth inside a range. In imbalance, one side is much more aggressive than the other. Price moves in one direction to find where the other side is willing to trade again, and a new balance forms there.

In the illustrative session above the first balance holds between 5,198.25 and 5,202.25 for five bars. Then three bars move price up 11.25 points with almost no overlap between them. That is the imbalance. From bar 9 onward the bars overlap again between 5,210.50 and 5,214.00: a new balance, higher than the first.

Seen as a volume profile, the same session looks like two hills with a valley between them. The hills are where the market spent time and traded a lot (the two balances). The valley is the imbalance leg, where price moved fast and little business was done. This picture comes up again and again in the track: a thin area on a profile is the fingerprint of an imbalance.

This links to what you know from the core course. The trend-and-range chapter (chapter 04) calls these phases "range" and "trend". Auction theory adds a reason for them, and the profile adds a way to measure them.

Rotations inside balance

While a market is balanced, price makes rotations: moves from one side of the range to the other. Each rotation probes an edge. If trade dries up past the edge, price comes back, and the balance is confirmed for now. Traders watch the edges because that is where the market is testing whether the old value still holds.

A breakout from balance is the opposite case. Price moves past the edge, keeps trading there, and the next bars build overlap and volume beyond it. That is acceptance, and it marks the start of an imbalance move. The difference between a probe that fails and a breakout that holds is mostly visible in what happens after the edge is crossed, which is why patience at value edges matters.

Initiative and responsive activity

Auction theory sorts trading activity by where it happens relative to value. Initiative activity trades away from value: buying above it or selling below it. It is the kind of activity that starts an imbalance. Responsive activity trades back toward value: buying below it, where prices look cheap, or selling above it, where prices look expensive. It is the kind of activity that keeps a market in balance.

Neither is good or bad. While a market stays in balance, probes of an edge come back, which is what balance means. When the initiative side is larger, value moves. The practical question on any edge test is therefore simple: which side is showing up? Order-flow tools (VP-08 and VP-09) give you a closer look at that question.

Day timeframe and other timeframe participants

Dalton's work popularised a second useful split: who is trading. Day timeframe participants trade within the session and are flat by the close. Other timeframe participants hold positions for days, weeks or longer. The day timeframe creates most of the back-and-forth. The other timeframe, when it arrives with size, is what moves value.

Day timeframe

Horizon: minutes to one session

What they care about: rotations inside the day's range

Typical footprint: many small trades inside value

Other timeframe

Horizon: days to months

What they care about: whether today's price is far from their idea of value

Typical footprint: larger, one-sided moves that shift value

You cannot see who is on the other side of your trade. What you can see is the footprint of their behaviour: a range that keeps rotating suggests mostly day-timeframe business, while a sustained, one-directional move that builds new value suggests other timeframe activity. Treat this as an interpretation of the chart, never as a fact about who traded.

Worked example: reading the illustrative session

  1. Bars 1 to 5: balance between 5,198.25 and 5,202.25. Every probe of an edge comes back. Responsive activity dominates.
  2. Bar 6: price closes at 5,205.25, above the balance high. That is initiative buying above value. The question is acceptance.
  3. Bars 7 and 8: price keeps trading higher with little overlap, and volume per bar is higher than during the balance (illustrative volumes 15,200 and 12,800 against about 8,000 to 9,000). The move is being accepted.
  4. Bars 9 to 12: overlap returns between 5,210.50 and 5,214.00. A new balance has formed higher. The old balance high at 5,202.25 becomes a reference for later: if price returns there, traders will watch whether it is accepted back inside the old value or rejected.

Common mistakes

  • Treating value as a fundamental fair price. In this framework value only means where trade happened. It moves every day.
  • Calling every edge touch a breakout. A probe past an edge is only initiative activity if it is accepted. Wait for trade to build beyond the edge.
  • Fading every move back to value. Responsive trading works while the market is balanced. In an imbalance, price can keep going far past what looks "expensive".
  • Claiming to know who is trading. "Other timeframe buyer" is a reading of behaviour, not information about identities.
  • Using theory instead of risk rules. Auction concepts help you choose where to act. Stops and position size still come from your risk plan (chapter 36).

Key takeaways

  • Auction market theory reads price as a search for the level where both sides will trade.
  • Value is where most trade happened. The value area and POC measure it.
  • Markets alternate between balance (rotation) and imbalance (one-directional search for new value).
  • Initiative activity trades away from value; responsive activity trades back toward it.
  • Acceptance (continued trade) and rejection (a quick return) are what you watch at every edge.

Practice exercises

  1. On a 30-minute ES chart, mark the last five days as "balance" or "imbalance". Write one sentence per day on what made you choose.
  2. Find one clear balance range. Count how many times price probed each edge and came back before the range broke.
  3. For the breakout that ended that range, describe the first two bars after the edge was crossed: overlapping or not, and did price trade back inside the old range?
  4. Add a session volume profile to the same days. Check that each balance shows up as a volume node and each imbalance as a thin area.

Self-check quiz

1. What does "value" mean in auction market theory?

The price range where most of the trading took place over a period, measured by time and volume. It is not a fundamental fair price.

2. What is the difference between balance and imbalance?

In balance, price rotates inside a range because both sides broadly agree on value. In imbalance, one side is more aggressive and price moves in one direction to find a new area where the other side will trade.

3. Is selling above value initiative or responsive?

Responsive. It trades back toward value from a price that looks expensive. Initiative selling happens below value.

4. Price moves above the value area high. What would you want to see to call that acceptance?

Continued trading above the edge, with overlapping bars and volume building there, rather than a quick return inside value.

5. Why does an imbalance leg show up as a thin area on a volume profile?

Price moved quickly through those prices in one direction, so little time was spent and little volume traded there.

Sources

  2. Volume profile indicators: basic concepts - TradingView Help Center
  3. Supported Matching Algorithms (how resting and aggressing orders trade) - CME Group Client Systems Wiki
  4. Time price opportunity charts explained - TradingView Help Center
  5. Mind Over Markets, Updated Edition (Dalton, Jones, Dalton; Wiley 2013) - further reading
  6. Markets and Market Logic (Steidlmayer, Koy; 1986) - further reading
